sources.title: Evaluation and Benchmarking of LLM Agents: A Survey
sources.venue: In Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2 (KDD '25), August 3–7, 2025, Toronto, ON, Canada.
sources.abstract: The rise of LLM-based agents has opened new frontiers in AI applications, yet evaluating these agents remains a complex and underdeveloped area. This survey provides an in-depth overview of the emerging field of LLM agent evaluation, introducing a two-dimensional taxonomy that organizes existing work along (1) evaluation objectives -- what to evaluate, such as agent behavior, capabilities, reliability, and safety -- and (2) evaluation process -- how to evaluate, including interaction modes, datasets and benchmarks, metric computation methods, and tooling. In addition to taxonomy, we highlight enterprise-specific challenges, such as role-based access to data, the need for reliability guarantees, dynamic and long-horizon interactions, and compliance, which are often overlooked in current research. We also identify future research directions, including holistic, more realistic, and scalable evaluation. This work aims to bring clarity to the fragmented landscape of agent evaluation and provide a framework for systematic assessment, enabling researchers and practitioners to evaluate LLM agents for real-world deployment.
sources.summary: Mohammadi, Li, Lo, and Yip survey how LLM agents are evaluated and draw a two-axis map: what to measure, and how the measurement is run. The paper is a taxonomy, not an experiment, and the figure's leaf names do not all match the section headings.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Mohammadi, Li, Lo, and Yip survey evaluation of LLM agents, systems that use a language model to reason, plan, and act. The paper is a map, not a new benchmark and not a leaderboard. It is useful for Part 1, which has to say why scoring one final answer is a weak test of an agent, and for Part 2, which has to choose among rules, a model judge, an agent judge, and a human. The four future-work items at the end line up with Part 4's open problems: coverage, realism, scale, and cost.

## What they did

They propose a two-dimensional taxonomy. The first dimension is the objective, what is being evaluated. The section headings are agent behavior, agent capabilities, reliability, and safety. Behavior is the outcome a user would notice: task completion, output quality, latency, and cost. Capabilities are the process: tool use, planning, memory, and multi-agent collaboration. In this survey, tool use means one call, including whether a call was needed, which tool, which parameter names, and which parameter values. Planning is the sequence. Reliability splits into consistency, repeating the same task, and robustness, surviving a changed input or environment. They define pass@k as success at least once in k attempts, and pass^k, from the τ benchmark, as success on all k attempts. They argue that pass^k matches mission-critical use better. They do not measure either one.

The second dimension is the process, how the evaluation is run. Section 4 has five branches: interaction mode, data, how the metric is computed, tooling, and context. Interaction mode is offline, a fixed dataset, against online, a live or simulated environment. Metric computation is the distinction this tutorial keeps using. Code-based checks are rules, tests, and assertions. LLM-as-a-judge scores from an instruction. Agent-as-a-judge, which they treat as a recent extension, uses further agents to refine the assessment. Human review is what they call the gold standard for subjective and safety-critical judgments, and they call it expensive. Context is the environment: a mock API, a sandbox, a web simulator, or the live system.

{{figure:fig1-taxonomy.png}}

## What they found

There is no experiment, so there is no success rate of theirs to quote. The contribution is the map, and the map is not perfectly stable inside the paper. Figure 1 labels the middle behavior branch "Interaction Quality." Section 3 and Table 1 call it output quality. Figure 1's reliability leaves are robustness, hallucinations, and error handling. The section and the table use consistency and robustness, and they do not give hallucinations their own heading. Figure 1's metric leaves are code-based, human-as-a-judge, and LLM-as-a-judge. The section adds agent-as-a-judge and calls the human case human-in-the-loop. The abstract's process list also drops evaluation context, which Figure 1 and Section 4.5 both include.

Table 1 is the objective side only. It pairs each category with metric names and with papers that use them. It is a set of examples, not a count of the literature. The reference list runs to 127, and the authors never say how many papers were included or what the inclusion rule was.

{{figure:table1-objectives.png}}

The enterprise section is an argument, not a measurement. They say current evaluations often miss role-based access, a guarantee of repeated success, long interactions, and policy constraints such as GDPR or HIPAA. They do not fill those gaps with numbers. The last section names four directions: evaluate the dimensions together, use more realistic settings, automate with simulators and judges, and bound time and cost.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 1 can use the behavior-versus-capability split. Task completion is the outcome. Tool choice, parameter names, and parameter values are a different question, and this survey puts them under capabilities.
- pass@k and pass^k are definitions worth keeping. One success in k tries is not the same measurement as success on all k tries. The survey defines them and does not report a value.
- Part 2's menu is already in their process axis: code, an LLM judge, an agent judge, and a human. They state the usual trade, consistency against coverage, and they do not compare the four on one task.
- Offline and online are the industry lifecycle in miniature. A fixed dataset and a live monitor are different evaluations, and they say the dataset is the cheaper and less faithful of the two, without a table that shows the gap.
- Latency and cost sit under behavior, next to success. A leaderboard that reports only success has dropped two of their behavior metrics.

## Limits

No new metric, no head-to-head, and no count of what was left out. Short-horizon benchmarks are argued to miss drift and cumulative effects. That is not shown here. The phrase "current agents struggle with consistency" cites τ-bench and reprints no pass^k. Safety is described as something that should have a numeric rate, and no rate is given. Read Figure 1 next to Table 1. The leaves are not the same list.

Process branches into interaction mode, data, metrics, tooling, and context. Reliability's leaves on this figure are Robustness, Hallucinations, and Error Handling. The metrics leaves are Code Based, Human-as-a-Judge, and LLM-as-a-Judge.

The consistency metric cell names pass^k and τ-Bench.

sources.title: Evaluating LLM-based Agents for Multi-Turn Conversations: A Survey
sources.abstract: This survey examines evaluation methods for large language model (LLM)-based agents in multi-turn conversational settings. Using a PRISMA-inspired framework, we systematically reviewed nearly 250 scholarly sources, capturing the state of the art from various venues of publication, and establishing a solid foundation for our analysis. Our study offers a structured approach by developing two interrelated taxonomy systems: one that defines \emph{what to evaluate} and another that explains \emph{how to evaluate}. The first taxonomy identifies key components of LLM-based agents for multi-turn conversations and their evaluation dimensions, including task completion, response quality, user experience, memory and context retention, as well as planning and tool integration. These components ensure that the performance of conversational agents is assessed in a holistic and meaningful manner. The second taxonomy system focuses on the evaluation methodologies. It categorizes approaches into annotation-based evaluations, automated metrics, hybrid strategies that combine human assessments with quantitative measures, and self-judging methods utilizing LLMs. This framework not only captures traditional metrics derived from language understanding, such as BLEU and ROUGE scores, but also incorporates advanced techniques that reflect the dynamic, interactive nature of multi-turn dialogues.
sources.summary: Survey of evaluating agents in multi-turn conversation. Relevant because the hands-on cases are short dialogues, and because a single-turn score misses later turns.

sources.title: A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge
sources.abstract: Accurate and consistent evaluation is crucial for decision-making across numerous fields, yet it remains a challenging task due to inherent subjectivity, variability, and scale. Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, leading to the emergence of "LLM-as-a-Judge," where LLMs are employed as evaluators for complex tasks. With their ability to process diverse data types and provide scalable, cost-effective, and consistent assessments, LLMs present a compelling alternative to traditional expert-driven evaluations. However, ensuring the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge systems remains a significant challenge that requires careful design and standardization. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of LLM-as-a-Judge, addressing the core question: How can reliable LLM-as-a-Judge systems be built? We explore strategies to enhance reliability, including improving consistency, mitigating biases, and adapting to diverse assessment scenarios. Additionally, we propose methodologies for evaluating the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge systems, supported by a novel benchmark designed for this purpose. To advance the development and real-world deployment of LLM-as-a-Judge systems, we also discussed practical applications, challenges, and future directions. This survey serves as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners in this rapidly evolving field.
sources.summary: Survey of the LLM-as-a-judge literature, cited from Part 2. It is the map of criteria, prompts, and known failure modes behind the tutorial’s judge section.

sources.title: From Generation to Judgment: Opportunities and Challenges of LLM-as-a-judge
sources.abstract: Assessment and evaluation have long been critical challenges in artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP). Traditional methods, usually matching-based or small model-based, often fall short in open-ended and dynamic scenarios. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) inspire the "LLM-as-a-judge" paradigm, where LLMs are leveraged to perform scoring, ranking, or selection for various machine learning evaluation scenarios. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of LLM-based judgment and assessment, offering an in-depth overview to review this evolving field. We first provide the definition from both input and output perspectives. Then we introduce a systematic taxonomy to explore LLM-as-a-judge along three dimensions: what to judge, how to judge, and how to benchmark. Finally, we also highlight key challenges and promising future directions for this emerging area. More resources on LLM-as-a-judge are on the website: this https URL and this https URL .
sources.summary: Survey of the shift from generating text to judging it. Background for Part 2: a judge is a model used as a measurement instrument, with its own errors.

sources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
sources.venue: In International Conference on Learning Representations. arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.03629.
sources.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across tasks in language understanding and interactive decision making, their abilities for reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought prompting) and acting (e.g. action plan generation) have primarily been studied as separate topics. In this paper, we explore the use of LLMs to generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner, allowing for greater synergy between the two: reasoning traces help the model induce, track, and update action plans as well as handle exceptions, while actions allow it to interface with external sources, such as knowledge bases or environments, to gather additional information. We apply our approach, named ReAct, to a diverse set of language and decision making tasks and demonstrate its effectiveness over state-of-the-art baselines, as well as improved human interpretability and trustworthiness over methods without reasoning or acting components. Concretely, on question answering (HotpotQA) and fact verification (Fever), ReAct overcomes issues of hallucination and error propagation prevalent in chain-of-thought reasoning by interacting with a simple Wikipedia API, and generates human-like task-solving trajectories that are more interpretable than baselines without reasoning traces. On two interactive decision making benchmarks (ALFWorld and WebShop), ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learning methods by an absolute success rate of 34% and 10% respectively, while being prompted with only one or two in-context examples. Project site with code: this https URL
sources.summary: The ReAct loop — reason, then act with a tool — is the practical agent definition on the Part 1 definitions slide. Evaluation has to look at those steps, not only the sentence at the end.

sources.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
sources.abstract: Language models (LMs) exhibit remarkable abilities to solve new tasks from just a few examples or textual instructions, especially at scale. They also, paradoxically, struggle with basic functionality, such as arithmetic or factual lookup, where much simpler and smaller models excel. In this paper, we show that LMs can teach themselves to use external tools via simple APIs and achieve the best of both worlds. We introduce Toolformer, a model trained to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to best incorporate the results into future token prediction. This is done in a self-supervised way, requiring nothing more than a handful of demonstrations for each API. We incorporate a range of tools, including a calculator, a Q\&A system, two different search engines, a translation system, and a calendar. Toolformer achieves substantially improved zero-shot performance across a variety of downstream tasks, often competitive with much larger models, without sacrificing its core language modeling abilities.
sources.summary: Early tool-use paper: the model decides when to call a tool and with what arguments. That is the behaviour Part 3 asks participants to judge, separately from the prose of the reply.

sources.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
sources.abstract: Existing benchmarks do not test language agents on their interaction with human users or ability to follow domain-specific rules, both of which are vital for deploying them in real world applications. We propose $\tau$-bench, a benchmark emulating dynamic conversations between a user (simulated by language models) and a language agent provided with domain-specific API tools and policy guidelines. We employ an efficient and faithful evaluation process that compares the database state at the end of a conversation with the annotated goal state. We also propose a new metric (pass^k) to evaluate the reliability of agent behavior over multiple trials. Our experiments show that even state-of-the-art function calling agents (like gpt-4o) succeed on <50% of the tasks, and are quite inconsistent (pass^8 <25% in retail). Our findings point to the need for methods that can improve the ability of agents to act consistently and follow rules reliably.
sources.summary: A benchmark where a tool-using agent has to converse with a simulated user and follow a policy. It is a picture of the kind of scenario the hands-on exercise is a small version of.

sources.title: τ^2-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
sources.abstract: Existing benchmarks for conversational AI agents simulate single-control environments, where only the AI agent can use tools to interact with the world, while the user remains a passive information provider. This differs from real-world scenarios like technical support, where users need to actively participate in modifying the state of the (shared) world. In order to address this gap, we introduce $\tau^2$-bench, with four key contributions: 1) A novel Telecom dual-control domain modeled as a Dec-POMDP, where both agent and user make use of tools to act in a shared, dynamic environment that tests both agent coordination and communication, 2) A compositional task generator that programmatically creates diverse, verifiable tasks from atomic components, ensuring domain coverage and controlled complexity, 3) A reliable user simulator tightly coupled with the environment, whose behavior is constrained by tools and observable states, improving simulation fidelity, 4) Fine-grained analysis of agent performance through multiple ablations including separating errors arising from reasoning vs communication/coordination. In particular, our experiments show significant performance drops when agents shift from no-user to dual-control, highlighting the challenges of guiding users. Overall, $\tau^2$-bench provides a controlled testbed for agents that must both reason effectively and guide user actions.
sources.summary: τ²-bench scores conversational agents in a telecom setting where the user and the agent both call tools on a shared world. Success is a set of assertions on the final state, not an LLM judge, and pass^1 on telecom is far below retail for the same models.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Barres, Dong, Ray, Si, and Narasimhan extend τ-bench from a conversation where only the agent acts to one where the user acts too. The new domain is telecom support: the user's phone is a set of tools, and the agent's account system is another set, and both write the same world. Part 1 needs this distinction. A final database that looks right is not the same fact as a trajectory you would trust, and one run is not yet a measurement. The score they report is pass^k, the fraction of k independent runs that succeed.

## What they did

Retail (115 tasks) and airline (50 tasks) stay single-control, as in the earlier benchmark. Telecom adds user tools: 15 that write and 15 that read, against the agent's 6 write and 7 read tools. Tasks are built from atomic subtasks, service, mobile data, and MMS, composed so that the assertions pass only after the full solution. The generator yields 2,285 tasks. The reported results use a balanced subsample of 114.

Success in telecom is assertion functions on the final world state. The paper does not name an LLM as the scorer. The user, though, is an LLM, gpt-4.1 for every run, following a persona that is empty, easy, or hard. Agents are gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, o4-mini, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet, at temperature 0, four runs per task. Two ablations, on gpt-4.1 and o4-mini only, pull the collaboration apart. In no-user mode the agent receives a ticket and controls every tool, including the ones the user would have called. In oracle-plan mode the agent is given the solution's tool sequence and still has to carry it out with the user.

{{figure:fig2-trajectory.png}}

## What they found

Figure 3 prints pass^k. For gpt-4.1, pass^1 is 0.74 on retail, 0.56 on airline, and 0.34 on telecom. At k = 4 those fall to 0.53, 0.40, and 0.19. The other three models show the same shape: telecom is the low bar, and the bar drops as k grows. Claude 3.7 Sonnet's telecom pass^1 is 0.49, close to its airline pass^1 of 0.50, and its telecom pass^4 is 0.25.

Figure 4 is the ablation, pass^1 on telecom. Under the original policy, gpt-4.1 goes from 0.52 with no user, to 0.34 in the default dual-control setting, to 0.73 with an oracle plan. o4-mini goes from 0.67, to 0.42, to 0.96. The paper calls the no-user to default change an 18-point drop and a 25-point drop. A more specific workflow policy raises default and no-user, and it lowers the oracle-plan scores, 0.73 to 0.57 for gpt-4.1 and 0.96 to 0.88 for o4-mini. Giving the agent the ground-truth sequence and a more detailed policy at the same time made the agent worse.

{{figure:fig3-passk.png}}

{{figure:fig4-modes.png}}

A manual look at the user simulator finds errors on 16% of 50 telecom conversations, 6% of them critical, against 40% of retail conversations and 47% of airline ones (Table 2). The telecom errors they list are all a premature transfer to a human.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- The score is a rule on the final state. Part 1's point stands even so: the same assertions fail much more often when the user has to act, so the trajectory, not only the end state, is doing the work.
- pass^k makes the reliability visible. gpt-4.1's telecom success falls from 0.34 at one run to 0.19 when all four runs must succeed. A single demo is a weaker measurement than the paper's own metric.
- Splitting reasoning from collaboration is a useful ablation for Part 3. No-user mode is the agent with every tool. Default mode is the agent that must ask the user to use theirs. The gap is large for both models tested.
- An oracle plan does not remove the need for the conversation, and a more detailed policy can hurt the agent that already has the plan. More instructions are not automatically a better evaluation.
- The user simulator is itself a model, and it makes mistakes. A failed task is not automatically an agent failure. They measured that, at 6% critical on the telecom sample they read.

## Limits

Retail and airline never receive user tools. The authors say they have not tried. Results are the 114-task subsample, not the 2,285 generated tasks. The workflow policy is pass^1 only, and only for two models. Figure 5, success against the number of actions, does not print a value per bin. The prose says default-mode pass^1 is close to zero beyond seven actions. No LLM judge grades these tasks, so the paper does not say how a judge would have scored the same traces.

figures.alt: A telecom conversation split by a dashed line. On the left the user checks a status bar and toggles mobile data with user tools. On the right the agent reads line details, sees roaming disabled, and enables roaming with agent tools. The caption says the user's phone state changes because the agent wrote the shared world.
figures.caption: Figure 2 from Barres et al. (2025). Dual control: the user and the agent both call tools, and the agent's write changes what the user's phone can do.

figures.alt: Four grouped bar charts of pass^k for k from 1 to 4, for gpt-4.1, o4-mini, gpt-4.1-mini, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet. Retail is blue, airline orange, telecom green. gpt-4.1 at k=1 is 0.74, 0.56, and 0.34. At k=4 those are 0.53, 0.40, and 0.19.
figures.caption: Figure 3 from Barres et al. (2025). Telecom is the low bar, and pass^k falls as more runs must all succeed.

figures.alt: Two bar charts of telecom pass^1 for gpt-4.1 and o4-mini. Modes are default, no-user, and oracle-plan. Under the original policy the bars are 0.34 and 0.42, then 0.52 and 0.67, then 0.73 and 0.96. Under the workflow policy, oracle-plan drops to 0.57 and 0.88.
figures.caption: Figure 4 from Barres et al. (2025). Taking the user out of the loop raises pass^1. A more detailed policy then hurts the agent that was given the solution.

sources.title: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation of Large Language Models
sources.venue: In Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, volume 267 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, pages 48371–48392.
sources.abstract: Function calling, also called tool use, refers to an LLM’s ability to invoke external functions, APIs, or user-defined tools in response to user queries—an essential capability for agentic LLM applications. Despite its prominence, there did not exist a standard benchmark to evaluate function calling abilities, due to two reasons – the challenging nature of evaluating when a function call is valid, and the challenge of acquiring diverse, real-world functions. We present the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL), a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate function calling capabilities in a wide range of real-world settings. The BFCL benchmark evaluates serial and parallel function calls, across various programming languages using a novel Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) evaluation method that can easily scale to thousands of functions. We construct the benchmark using a combination of expert curated, and user-contributed functions and associated prompts. Finally, BFCL benchmark evaluates the ability of models to abstain and reason in stateful multi-step agentic setting. Evaluating a wide range of models, we observe that while state-of-the-art LLMs excel at singleturn calls, memory, dynamic decision-making, and long-horizon reasoning remain open challenges. Since its preview, BFCL has become the defacto standard for evaluating function-calls, and can be accessed at gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/leaderboard.html.
sources.summary: A standard benchmark for whether a model emits a valid tool call, including multi-step calls. Part 1 and Part 3 both need this distinction: checking the call can be deterministic, while judging the advice often cannot.

sources.title: ToolSandbox: A Stateful, Conversational, Interactive Evaluation Benchmark for LLM Tool Use Capabilities
sources.abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) advancements sparked a growing research interest in tool assisted LLMs solving real-world challenges, which calls for comprehensive evaluation of tool-use capabilities. While previous works focused on either evaluating over stateless web services (RESTful API), based on a single turn user prompt, or an off-policy dialog trajectory, ToolSandbox includes stateful tool execution, implicit state dependencies between tools, a built-in user simulator supporting on-policy conversational evaluation and a dynamic evaluation strategy for intermediate and final milestones over an arbitrary trajectory. We show that open source and proprietary models have a significant performance gap, and complex tasks like State Dependency, Canonicalization and Insufficient Information defined in ToolSandbox are challenging even the most capable SOTA LLMs, providing brand-new insights into tool-use LLM capabilities. ToolSandbox evaluation framework is released at this https URL
sources.summary: A stateful, conversational benchmark for tool use. Relevant where the tutorial contrasts a single tool call with an interaction that depends on earlier state.
sources.note: arXiv id 2408.04682 is a 2024 submission. The reading checklist dates the paper 2025.

sources.title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
sources.abstract: Recent advances in Language Model (LM) agents and tool use, exemplified by applications like ChatGPT Plugins, enable a rich set of capabilities but also amplify potential risks - such as leaking private data or causing financial losses. Identifying these risks is labor-intensive, necessitating implementing the tools, setting up the environment for each test scenario manually, and finding risky cases. As tools and agents become more complex, the high cost of testing these agents will make it increasingly difficult to find high-stakes, long-tailed risks. To address these challenges, we introduce ToolEmu: a framework that uses an LM to emulate tool execution and enables the testing of LM agents against a diverse range of tools and scenarios, without manual instantiation. Alongside the emulator, we develop an LM-based automatic safety evaluator that examines agent failures and quantifies associated risks. We test both the tool emulator and evaluator through human evaluation and find that 68.8% of failures identified with ToolEmu would be valid real-world agent failures. Using our curated initial benchmark consisting of 36 high-stakes tools and 144 test cases, we provide a quantitative risk analysis of current LM agents and identify numerous failures with potentially severe outcomes. Notably, even the safest LM agent exhibits such failures 23.9% of the time according to our evaluator, underscoring the need to develop safer LM agents for real-world deployment.
sources.summary: Uses a language model to emulate tools so agent risks can be tested without live APIs. Connects Part 1 (risks, red-teaming) with the idea that the test harness is itself a model.
sources.note: The arXiv submission is 2023 (2309.15817). The reading checklist dates it 2024.

sources.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
sources.abstract: The potential of Large Language Model (LLM) as agents has been widely acknowledged recently. Thus, there is an urgent need to quantitatively \textit{evaluate LLMs as agents} on challenging tasks in interactive environments. We present AgentBench, a multi-dimensional benchmark that consists of 8 distinct environments to assess LLM-as-Agent's reasoning and decision-making abilities. Our extensive test over \num API-based and open-sourced (OSS) LLMs shows that, while top commercial LLMs present a strong ability of acting as agents in complex environments, there is a significant disparity in performance between them and many OSS competitors that are no larger than 70B. We identify the typical reasons of failures in environments and LLMs, showing that poor long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction following abilities are the main obstacles for developing usable LLM agents. Improving instruction following and training on high quality multi-round alignment data could improve agent performance. And different from existing assumptions, training on code present ambivalent impacts on different agent tasks. Datasets, environments, and an integrated evaluation package for AgentBench are released at this https URL .
sources.summary: A multi-environment benchmark of LLMs as agents. Use it as an example of outcome-style agent eval, which Part 1 argues is not the whole measurement.
sources.note: arXiv id 2308.03688 is a 2023 submission. The reading checklist dates the paper 2024.

sources.title: AgentBoard: An Analytical Evaluation Board of Multi-turn LLM Agents
sources.abstract: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) as general-purpose agents is essential for understanding their capabilities and facilitating their integration into practical applications. However, the evaluation process presents substantial challenges. A primary obstacle is the benchmarking of agent performance across diverse scenarios within a unified framework, especially in maintaining partially-observable environments and ensuring multi-round interactions. Moreover, current evaluation frameworks mostly focus on the final success rate, revealing few insights during the process and failing to provide a deep understanding of the model abilities. To address these challenges, we introduce AgentBoard, a pioneering comprehensive benchmark and accompanied open-source evaluation framework tailored to analytical evaluation of LLM agents. AgentBoard offers a fine-grained progress rate metric that captures incremental advancements as well as a comprehensive evaluation toolkit that features easy assessment of agents for multi-faceted analysis. This not only sheds light on the capabilities and limitations of LLM agents but also propels the interpretability of their performance to the forefront. Ultimately, AgentBoard serves as a step towards demystifying agent behaviors and accelerating the development of stronger LLM agents.
sources.summary: An analysis board for multi-turn agents, not only a single score. Supports the Part 1 point that you want to see progress along a trajectory.

sources.title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
sources.abstract: We introduce GAIA, a benchmark for General AI Assistants that, if solved, would represent a milestone in AI research. GAIA proposes real-world questions that require a set of fundamental abilities such as reasoning, multi-modality handling, web browsing, and generally tool-use proficiency. GAIA questions are conceptually simple for humans yet challenging for most advanced AIs: we show that human respondents obtain 92\% vs. 15\% for GPT-4 equipped with plugins. This notable performance disparity contrasts with the recent trend of LLMs outperforming humans on tasks requiring professional skills in e.g. law or chemistry. GAIA's philosophy departs from the current trend in AI benchmarks suggesting to target tasks that are ever more difficult for humans. We posit that the advent of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) hinges on a system's capability to exhibit similar robustness as the average human does on such questions. Using GAIA's methodology, we devise 466 questions and their answer. We release our questions while retaining answers to 300 of them to power a leader-board available at this https URL .
sources.summary: A benchmark of questions that need tools and several steps, scored mostly on the final answer. A clear example of the outcome-only eval Part 1 says is not enough for agents.

sources.title: AI Agents That Matter
sources.abstract: AI agents are an exciting new research direction, and agent development is driven by benchmarks. Our analysis of current agent benchmarks and evaluation practices reveals several shortcomings that hinder their usefulness in real-world applications. First, there is a narrow focus on accuracy without attention to other metrics. As a result, SOTA agents are needlessly complex and costly, and the community has reached mistaken conclusions about the sources of accuracy gains. Our focus on cost in addition to accuracy motivates the new goal of jointly optimizing the two metrics. We design and implement one such optimization, showing its potential to greatly reduce cost while maintaining accuracy. Second, the benchmarking needs of model and downstream developers have been conflated, making it hard to identify which agent would be best suited for a particular application. Third, many agent benchmarks have inadequate holdout sets, and sometimes none at all. This has led to agents that are fragile because they take shortcuts and overfit to the benchmark in various ways. We prescribe a principled framework for avoiding overfitting. Finally, there is a lack of standardization in evaluation practices, leading to a pervasive lack of reproducibility. We hope that the steps we introduce for addressing these shortcomings will spur the development of agents that are useful in the real world and not just accurate on benchmarks.
sources.summary: Argues that many agent benchmarks overstate capability because of cost, shortcuts, and evaluation design. Directly useful in Part 1 and Part 4 when discussing whether a number on a leaderboard is a real eval.

sources.title: Evaluation-Driven Development and Operations of LLM Agents: A Process Model and Reference Architecture
sources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled the emergence of LLM agents, systems capable of pursuing under-specified goals and adapting after deployment. Evaluating such agents is challenging because their behavior is open ended, probabilistic, and shaped by system-level interactions over time. Traditional evaluation methods, built around fixed benchmarks and static test suites, fail to capture emergent behaviors or support continuous adaptation across the lifecycle. To ground a more systematic approach, we conduct a multivocal literature review (MLR) synthesizing academic and industrial evaluation practices. The findings directly inform two empirically derived artifacts: a process model and a reference architecture that embed evaluation as a continuous, governing function rather than a terminal checkpoint. Together they constitute the evaluation-driven development and operations (EDDOps) approach, which unifies offline (development-time) and online (runtime) evaluation within a closed feedback loop. By making evaluation evidence drive both runtime adaptation and governed redevelopment, EDDOps supports safer, more traceable evolution of LLM agents aligned with changing objectives, user needs, and governance constraints.
sources.summary: Proposes a process and a reference architecture where offline and online evaluation drive how an agent is changed. This is the industry lifecycle on the Part 1 agenda: datasets, versioning, and monitoring, not a single test run.
sources.note: arXiv submission 2024, revised through 2025. The checklist writes 2024–2025.

sources.title: AgentOps: Enabling Observability of LLM Agents
sources.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains, gaining extensive attention from academia and industry. However, these agents raise significant concerns on AI safety due to their autonomous and non-deterministic behavior, as well as continuous evolving nature . From a DevOps perspective, enabling observability in agents is necessary to ensuring AI safety, as stakeholders can gain insights into the agents' inner workings, allowing them to proactively understand the agents, detect anomalies, and prevent potential failures. Therefore, in this paper, we present a comprehensive taxonomy of AgentOps, identifying the artifacts and associated data that should be traced throughout the entire lifecycle of agents to achieve effective observability. The taxonomy is developed based on a systematic mapping study of existing AgentOps tools. Our taxonomy serves as a reference template for developers to design and implement AgentOps infrastructure that supports monitoring, logging, and analytics. thereby ensuring AI safety.
sources.summary: A taxonomy of what to trace across an agent’s life so someone can see what it did. Matches the Part 1 observability slide: monitoring, reporting, and kill switches need a trace.

sources.title: Who Validates the Validators? Aligning LLM-Assisted Evaluation of LLM Outputs with Human Preferences
sources.abstract: Due to the cumbersome nature of human evaluation and limitations of code-based evaluation, Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to assist humans in evaluating LLM outputs. Yet LLM-generated evaluators simply inherit all the problems of the LLMs they evaluate, requiring further human validation. We present a mixed-initiative approach to ``validate the validators'' -- aligning LLM-generated evaluation functions (be it prompts or code) with human requirements. Our interface, EvalGen, provides automated assistance to users in generating evaluation criteria and implementing assertions. While generating candidate implementations (Python functions, LLM grader prompts), EvalGen asks humans to grade a subset of LLM outputs; this feedback is used to select implementations that better align with user grades. A qualitative study finds overall support for EvalGen but underscores the subjectivity and iterative process of alignment. In particular, we identify a phenomenon we dub \emph{criteria drift}: users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps users define criteria. What is more, some criteria appears \emph{dependent} on the specific LLM outputs observed (rather than independent criteria that can be defined \emph{a priori}), raising serious questions for approaches that assume the independence of evaluation from observation of model outputs. We present our interface and implementation details, a comparison of our algorithm with a baseline approach, and implications for the design of future LLM evaluation assistants.
sources.summary: Studies how to align a model-based evaluator with human preferences, including who checks the checker. Core Part 2 and Part 4 material: a judge is not self-justifying.

sources.title: Building Your Own Product Copilot: Challenges, Opportunities, and Needs
sources.abstract: A race is underway to embed advanced AI capabilities into products. These product copilots enable users to ask questions in natural language and receive relevant responses that are specific to the user's context. In fact, virtually every large technology company is looking to add these capabilities to their software products. However, for most software engineers, this is often their first encounter with integrating AI-powered technology. Furthermore, software engineering processes and tools have not caught up with the challenges and scale involved with building AI-powered applications. In this work, we present the findings of an interview study with 26 professional software engineers responsible for building product copilots at various companies. From our interviews, we found pain points at every step of the engineering process and the challenges that strained existing development practices. We then conducted group brainstorming sessions to collaborative on opportunities and tool designs for the broader software engineering community.
sources.summary: Field study of teams building product copilots, including what evaluation support they lack. Grounds the Part 1 claim that evals are an engineering workflow, not only a paper benchmark.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
sources.abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) based chat assistants is challenging due to their broad capabilities and the inadequacy of existing benchmarks in measuring human preferences. To address this, we explore using strong LLMs as judges to evaluate these models on more open-ended questions. We examine the usage and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, as well as limited reasoning ability, and propose solutions to mitigate some of them. We then verify the agreement between LLM judges and human preferences by introducing two benchmarks: MT-bench, a multi-turn question set; and Chatbot Arena, a crowdsourced battle platform. Our results reveal that strong LLM judges like GPT-4 can match both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences well, achieving over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans. Hence, LLM-as-a-judge is a scalable and explainable way to approximate human preferences, which are otherwise very expensive to obtain. Additionally, we show our benchmark and traditional benchmarks complement each other by evaluating several variants of LLaMA and Vicuna. The MT-bench questions, 3K expert votes, and 30K conversations with human preferences are publicly available at this https URL .
sources.summary: The paper that established LLM-as-a-judge against human preferences on MT-Bench and arena votes. Cited from the Part 1 metrics slide and the Part 2 source list as the basic method the tutorial then complicates.

sources.title: G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
sources.abstract: The quality of texts generated by natural language generation (NLG) systems is hard to measure automatically. Conventional reference-based metrics, such as BLEU and ROUGE, have been shown to have relatively low correlation with human judgments, especially for tasks that require creativity and diversity. Recent studies suggest using large language models (LLMs) as reference-free metrics for NLG evaluation, which have the benefit of being applicable to new tasks that lack human references. However, these LLM-based evaluators still have lower human correspondence than medium-size neural evaluators. In this work, we present G-Eval, a framework of using large language models with chain-of-thoughts (CoT) and a form-filling paradigm, to assess the quality of NLG outputs. We experiment with two generation tasks, text summarization and dialogue generation. We show that G-Eval with GPT-4 as the backbone model achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.514 with human on summarization task, outperforming all previous methods by a large margin. We also propose preliminary analysis on the behavior of LLM-based evaluators, and highlight the potential issue of LLM-based evaluators having a bias towards the LLM-generated texts. The code is at this https URL
sources.summary: A judge that applies a form-filling rubric with a chain of thought. A concrete Part 2 pattern for the hands-on prompt: criteria, steps, then a score.

sources.title: Prometheus: Inducing Fine-grained Evaluation Capability in Language Models
sources.abstract: Recently, using a powerful proprietary Large Language Model (LLM) (e.g., GPT-4) as an evaluator for long-form responses has become the de facto standard. However, for practitioners with large-scale evaluation tasks and custom criteria in consideration (e.g., child-readability), using proprietary LLMs as an evaluator is unreliable due to the closed-source nature, uncontrolled versioning, and prohibitive costs. In this work, we propose Prometheus, a fully open-source LLM that is on par with GPT-4's evaluation capabilities when the appropriate reference materials (reference answer, score rubric) are accompanied. We first construct the Feedback Collection, a new dataset that consists of 1K fine-grained score rubrics, 20K instructions, and 100K responses and language feedback generated by GPT-4. Using the Feedback Collection, we train Prometheus, a 13B evaluator LLM that can assess any given long-form text based on customized score rubric provided by the user. Experimental results show that Prometheus scores a Pearson correlation of 0.897 with human evaluators when evaluating with 45 customized score rubrics, which is on par with GPT-4 (0.882), and greatly outperforms ChatGPT (0.392). Furthermore, measuring correlation with GPT-4 with 1222 customized score rubrics across four benchmarks (MT Bench, Vicuna Bench, Feedback Bench, Flask Eval) shows similar trends, bolstering Prometheus's capability as an evaluator LLM. Lastly, Prometheus achieves the highest accuracy on two human preference benchmarks (HHH Alignment & MT Bench Human Judgment) compared to open-sourced reward models explicitly trained on human preference datasets, highlighting its potential as an universal reward model. We open-source our code, dataset, and model at this https URL .
sources.summary: Trains an open evaluator against a fine-grained rubric. Relevant in Part 2 when discussing whether the judge is a prompted general model or a model built to score.
sources.note: arXiv submission 2023 (2310.08491). The reading checklist dates Prometheus 2024.

sources.title: Prometheus 2: An Open Source Language Model Specialized in Evaluating Other Language Models
sources.abstract: Proprietary LMs such as GPT-4 are often employed to assess the quality of responses from various LMs. However, concerns including transparency, controllability, and affordability strongly motivate the development of open-source LMs specialized in evaluations. On the other hand, existing open evaluator LMs exhibit critical shortcomings: 1) they issue scores that significantly diverge from those assigned by humans, and 2) they lack the flexibility to perform both direct assessment and pairwise ranking, the two most prevalent forms of assessment. Additionally, they do not possess the ability to evaluate based on custom evaluation criteria, focusing instead on general attributes like helpfulness and harmlessness. To address these issues, we introduce Prometheus 2, a more powerful evaluator LM than its predecessor that closely mirrors human and GPT-4 judgements. Moreover, it is capable of processing both direct assessment and pair-wise ranking formats grouped with a user-defined evaluation criteria. On four direct assessment benchmarks and four pairwise ranking benchmarks, Prometheus 2 scores the highest correlation and agreement with humans and proprietary LM judges among all tested open evaluator LMs. Our models, code, and data are all publicly available at this https URL .
sources.summary: A follow-on open evaluator aimed at finer, more transferable scores. Same Part 2 use as Prometheus: rubrics can be compiled into a model, not only pasted into a prompt.

sources.title: HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health
sources.abstract: We present HealthBench, an open-source benchmark measuring the performance and safety of large language models in healthcare. HealthBench consists of 5,000 multi-turn conversations between a model and an individual user or healthcare professional. Responses are evaluated using conversation-specific rubrics created by 262 physicians. Unlike previous multiple-choice or short-answer benchmarks, HealthBench enables realistic, open-ended evaluation through 48,562 unique rubric criteria spanning several health contexts (e.g., emergencies, transforming clinical data, global health) and behavioral dimensions (e.g., accuracy, instruction following, communication). HealthBench performance over the last two years reflects steady initial progress (compare GPT-3.5 Turbo's 16% to GPT-4o's 32%) and more rapid recent improvements (o3 scores 60%). Smaller models have especially improved: GPT-4.1 nano outperforms GPT-4o and is 25 times cheaper. We additionally release two HealthBench variations: HealthBench Consensus, which includes 34 particularly important dimensions of model behavior validated via physician consensus, and HealthBench Hard, where the current top score is 32%. We hope that HealthBench grounds progress towards model development and applications that benefit human health.
sources.summary: HealthBench scores 5,000 health conversations with physician-written criteria, positive and negative points, and a GPT-4.1 judge that marks each criterion met or not. Overall scores run from about 0.16 to about 0.60, and the hard subset's top score is 0.32.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Arora, Wei, Hicks, and colleagues built HealthBench to score model replies in health conversations with a rubric a physician wrote for that conversation. It is not an agent benchmark and it has no tools. It is still the clearest public example of the Part 2 pattern: conversation-specific criteria, a point scale that can penalize, and a model judge that returns met or not met. Part 4's question, whether that judge agrees with physicians, is a section of the paper rather than an afterthought.

## What they did

The set is 5,000 conversations, single-turn or multi-turn, each ending on a user message. Most were synthesized from situation types physicians listed, some were red-team conversations, and some were rewritten from an existing health-search set. Each example has its own criteria. A criterion carries a nonzero point value from −10 to 10. Positive points reward something the reply should do. Negative points penalize a behavior when it is present. The grader is GPT-4.1. It scores each criterion independently as met or not met. Met awards the full point value, including a penalty. Not met awards zero.

The example score is the sum of awarded points divided by the sum of the positive point values only. A met penalty can pull an example below zero. The reported model score is the mean of example scores, clipped to the range 0 to 1. Table 3 counts 57,237 criterion instances: 49,184 written for that example and 8,053 occurrences of consensus criteria. The consensus criteria are a smaller shared set, attached when a majority of reviewers agreed the category applied. The paper says there are 34 unique consensus criteria. HealthBench Consensus scores 3,671 examples on the consensus criteria only. HealthBench Hard is 1,000 examples kept because several frontier models scored them poorly.

The physician cohort is 262 people, practicing in 60 countries, across 26 specialties. The model grader was chosen because, on the consensus criteria, it matched physician agreement without the cost of a reasoning model.

{{figure:fig1-infographic.png}}

## What they found

Section 6.1 and the abstract put the overall score at 16% for GPT-3.5 Turbo, 32% for GPT-4o, and 60% for o3. Table 7, sixteen runs, prints the means as 0.1554, 0.3233, and 0.5990. Run-to-run standard deviations are about 0.002. On the Consensus subset the order changes: GPT-4.1 at 0.9398 is above o3 at 0.9282 (Table 8). On the Hard subset, o3 scores 0.32 against its 0.60 overall. Figure 10 breaks Hard out by axis. Communication quality is the tall bar. Completeness is low, and for several weaker models the dashed overall score sits at or near zero.

Figure 1 is one worked example of the arithmetic. Criteria of +7, +5, and +10 are the positive pool, 22 points. The +5 criterion is missed. A −6 penalty is met. The displayed score is 11 out of 22, 50%. The denominator never includes the penalty, so a met penalty lowers the numerator only.

The grader study covers only consensus criteria: 60,896 physician grades of met or not met. Macro F1 treats "met" and "not met" equally. GPT-4.1's macro F1 is above the average physician in five of seven themes and below in health data tasks, 0.683 against 0.730, at the 37.5th percentile of physicians on that theme (Table 5). Across grader models, GPT-4.1 is the highest at 0.709 (Table 6). The authors note it was the model used while the prompt was tuned.

{{figure:fig4-frontier.png}}

{{figure:fig10-hard.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A rubric can be specific to the conversation, with points that reward and points that penalize. A met penalty lowers the score and is not added to the denominator.
- The judge is binary per criterion, and the example score is a sum. That is a different design from asking the model for one holistic number.
- Overall, Consensus, and Hard do not rank models the same way. o3 leads the full set and the hard slice. GPT-4.1 leads the consensus slice. Part 4 should not treat one headline number as the measurement.
- Judge–physician agreement is itself a result, and it is uneven. The grader beats the average physician on five themes and loses on health data tasks. A judge chosen because it was cheap can still be the one that was tuned against.

## Limits

These are single replies, not multi-step clinical work, and not tool use. The paper does not claim health outcomes. Meta-evaluation covers consensus criteria only. Example-specific criteria were written by individual physicians and not rechecked by others. The abstract's count of 48,562 unique criteria is not the same number as Table 3's 57,237 instances, and the paper does not show the arithmetic that connects them. The grading prompt is not printed. Physicians editing September 2024 references improved them more often than not, 56.2% against 39.8%. April 2025 references were a near tie, 46.8% improved against 47.7% worsened.

sources.title: Learning to Judge: LLMs Designing and Applying Evaluation Rubrics
sources.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2026. arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.08672.
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as evaluators for natural language generation, applying human-defined rubrics to assess system outputs. However, human rubrics are often static and misaligned with how models internally represent language quality. We introduce GER-Eval (Generating Evaluation Rubrics for Evaluation) to investigate whether LLMs can design and apply their own evaluation rubrics. We evaluate the semantic coherence and scoring reliability of LLM-defined criteria and their alignment with human criteria. LLMs reliably generate interpretable and task-aware evaluation dimensions and apply them consistently within models, but their scoring reliability degrades in factual and knowledge-intensive settings. Closed-source models such as GPT-4o achieve higher agreement and cross-model generalization than open-weight models such as Llama. Our findings position evaluation as a learned linguistic capability of LLMs, consistent within models but fragmented across them, and call for new methods that jointly model human and LLM evaluative language to improve reliability and interpretability.
sources.summary: Siro, Aliannejadi, and Aliannejadi test the assumption that a model-written rubric is a more reliable way to score text than a human rubric. Within one model the scores are often stable. Agreement with humans, and agreement across models, collapses on the factual biomedical summaries.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Siro, Aliannejadi, and Aliannejadi separate two jobs that Part 2 often runs together: who writes the rubric, and who applies it. GER-Eval is a diagnostic, not a new rubric generator. It asks whether a model-written rubric is more reliable than a human one, and whether a model applies either rubric the same way a person would. The datasets are summaries, dialogues, and instruction-following replies, not agent trajectories. The lesson still sits in Part 2 and Part 4. A rubric that sounds specific can score fluency and miss the facts.

## What they did

A criterion is a name, a description, and a scale, plus a short instruction for how to score it. Generation has three conditions: the task alone, the task plus example inputs, and the task plus a high-scoring and a low-scoring output. Application has two conditions, and the words mean something else there: rubric only, which they call zero-shot, and rubric plus demonstrations, which they call few-shot. Tables 3 and 4 compare those two application setups with each other. They are not agreement with humans. Table 5 is the table that correlates model scores with human scores, and it uses the human rubrics.

They take 50 items from each of four datasets: SummEval, HelpSteer2, USR, and SumPubMed. The judges are GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Mixtral-8x22B, and Qwen2.5-72B. Scoring is greedy. Rubric generation uses temperature 0.7. They also hand a rubric written by GPT-4o or by Llama to the other models, which is the transfer test.

{{figure:fig2-task-specific.png}}

## What they found

Models produce about five to eight criteria per dataset. Figure 2 shows the share the authors counted as task-specific under three generation prompts. The paper does not print those bar heights. What it does print is alignment with the human criteria, which is high on some datasets and often below 60% on SumPubMed.

The number that matters for the tutorial is Table 5, Spearman correlation with human scores when the model applies the human rubric. On the dialogue set, USR, every model lands between 0.77 and 0.82. On HelpSteer2 the range is 0.31 to 0.65. On SummEval it is 0.24 to 0.58. On the biomedical summaries, SumPubMed, it is −0.09 to 0.30. Few-shot demonstrations raise HelpSteer2 for four of the five models and do not rescue SumPubMed.

A high correlation between a model's own zero-shot and few-shot scores is a different fact. That within-model agreement can sit near 0.9 on USR in Table 4 while the correlation with humans in Table 5 is lower. On SumPubMed, GPT-4o's zero-shot and few-shot scores agree 92% of the time on its own rubrics (Table 3) with a correlation of only 0.53. Stable is not the same as valid.

{{figure:table5-human-spearman.png}}

Figure 4 is what happens when another model applies the rubric. On USR the Spearman values stay mostly positive and often high. On SumPubMed they sit near zero, with a few cells above 0.3 and some negative. Inter-rater reliability across models on the SumPubMed rubrics has every ICC below 0.2 (Tables 8 and 9).

{{figure:fig4-transfer.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Who writes the rubric is part of the measurement. Part 2 should not treat "let the model draft the criteria" as a free improvement over a human rubric. This paper does not show that self-written rubrics agree better with humans. Table 5 is the human-rubric result.
- A model can be consistent with itself and still disagree with people. Part 4's consistency check is not a validity check. The SumPubMed row is the example: high within-model agreement, correlation with humans at or below 0.30.
- The failure is sharper where the rubric needs facts. Dialogue quality transfers. Biomedical summary quality does not. A rubric for a tool-using agent that checks "did the tool argument match the request" is closer to the factual case than to the dialogue case.
- Few-shot scoring examples help on some datasets and not on others. They are not a general fix.
- Rubrics do not travel cleanly across models. A criterion written by one model and scored by another can lose the correlation even when each model is internally coherent.

## Limits

English text only, five models, 50 items per dataset, and no check of factual accuracy beyond the existing human scores. The study does not claim GER-Eval is a better rubric generator. One sentence in the results section describes human correlations of about 0.8 to 0.9 on HelpSteer2 and USR. Table 5, the human-score table, has USR at 0.77 to 0.82 and HelpSteer2 at 0.31 to 0.65. The higher band matches zero-shot versus few-shot agreement, not agreement with humans.

figures.alt: Grouped bars of the percent of generated rubrics counted as task-specific, for GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama, Mixtral, and Qwen. Three bars per model: task only, task plus examples, and task plus good/bad pairs. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 100.
figures.caption: Figure 2 from Siro et al. (2026). How often generated criteria were counted as task-specific. The paper does not print the bar heights in the text.

figures.caption: Table 5 from Siro et al. (2026). Correlation with humans when the model applies the human rubric. This is the validity table, not the within-model stability table.

figures.alt: Four heatmaps of Spearman correlation when one model applies another model's rubric. USR panels are mostly warm, from about 0.20 to 0.90. SumPubMed panels are near zero and include negative cells, with a color scale from −1 to 1.
figures.caption: Figure 4 from Siro et al. (2026). A rubric written by GPT-4o or Llama still correlates on dialogue and falls apart on biomedical summaries.

sources.title: From Rubrics to Reliable Scores: Evidence-Grounded Text Evaluation with LLM Judges
sources.abstract: Rubric-based text evaluation increasingly relies on large language models (LLMs) as scalable judges, yet frozen black-box models can interpret the same criteria inconsistently, produce score attributions that are difficult to audit, and map judgments poorly onto human scoring scales. We define this challenge as criteria transfer: translating human rubric intent into a stable, auditable inference-time scoring protocol. We introduce Rulers, which locks a task-level rubric specification, executes it through structured, evidence-grounded judgments, and calibrates the resulting signals to human score boundaries. Across four rubric-governed benchmarks and multiple frozen backbone models, Rulers achieves stronger agreement with human scores in most evaluated settings, while better matching empirical score distributions and remaining more stable under semantically equivalent rubric perturbations. Calibration controls and component ablations show that these gains cannot be attributed to post-hoc alignment alone, but depend on the combination of fixed criteria, traceable evidence, and calibrated score interpretation. These findings suggest that reliable LLM judging requires faithfully operationalizing human evaluation standards rather than relying on prompt-level scoring alone. Our code is available at this https URL .
sources.summary: RULERS keeps the judge frozen, locks one rubric bundle for the whole task, and forces each checklist decision to cite evidence before a small calibration set maps the scores onto the human scale. The gain in quadratic weighted kappa is large on two essay sets and is not the best score on every row.
sources.note: The reading checklist titles this RULERS: Locked Rubrics and Evidence-Anchored Scoring for Robust LLM Evaluation. The current arXiv page uses the title stored here. Same authors (Hong et al.).
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Hong, Yao, Shen, and colleagues name the problem as criteria transfer: a human rubric has to become a scoring procedure that lands on the human scale and can be audited. RULERS does that at inference time. It does not train the judge. The tasks are essays, summaries, and data-to-text, not agent trajectories. It belongs in Part 2, where a rubric and a scale are chosen, and in Part 4, where a score that moves because the prompt was reworded is a reliability failure.

## What they did

Three stages, drawn in Figure 1. Phase I compiles the human rubric once into a locked bundle: traits, a checklist, score anchors, evidence rules, and a hash. The same bundle is reused for every instance in the task. Phase II splits the input into sentences or paragraphs. The frozen judge marks each checklist item as absent, partial, or clearly present, coded 0, 1, or 2, and cites evidence. A trait score is the average of those decisions, scaled and clipped onto the trait's range. Phase III fits a ridge regression on structured signals, using N = 200 labeled calibration examples, then a monotone map onto the human score distribution. Both the regression and the map are frozen before the test split.

The metric is quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), mean plus or minus a bootstrap standard error. Baselines are direct holistic scoring, multi-trait scoring, AutoScore, and CheckEval, all at temperature 0, without the RULERS calibration layer in the main table. Backbones are GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.1-70B. Datasets are ASAP 2.0 (argument essays, scores 1–6, 7,421 test essays), SummHF (summaries, 1–7), DREsS (learner essays, 3–15), and WebNLG (data-to-text). WebNLG has no single human overall score, so the target is the sum of semantics, grammar, and fluency, which gives the range 3–9.

{{figure:fig1-pipeline.png}}

## What they found

Table 2 is the comparison. RULERS is the highest QWK in every row except the two SummHF rows that use Llama. The highest cell is Llama-3.1-70B on ASAP 2.0, 0.7179 ± 0.0055, against 0.4804 ± 0.0079 for direct holistic scoring with the same backbone. On DREsS the RULERS scores sit near 0.53 to 0.56 while the baselines are mostly under 0.37. On SummHF with Llama-3.1-8B, CheckEval is 0.2594 ± 0.0276 and RULERS is 0.2060 ± 0.0318. With Llama-3.1-70B, CheckEval is 0.4606 ± 0.0256 and RULERS is 0.4454 ± 0.0315. A larger backbone is not always a higher QWK.

Figure 2 compares score shapes with the human histogram. The paper does not print a distance between the curves. The claim in the text is that RULERS more often keeps the center and the spread of the human scores. Table 5 separates two gains on GPT-4o-mini at N = 200. Calibrating the direct holistic score helps on all four datasets. A further gap from that calibrated baseline to RULERS remains: +0.1664 on ASAP 2.0, +0.0329 on SummHF, +0.1844 on DREsS, and +0.0527 on WebNLG. At N = 100 on SummHF, the calibrated direct score beats RULERS. The "calibration is not the whole story" claim is the N = 200 table, not every cell.

{{figure:table2-qwk.png}}

{{figure:fig2-distributions.png}}

Dropping any phase lowers QWK on all four datasets for GPT-4o-mini (Table 4). Token counts, reported only for GPT-4o-mini, put RULERS above a single-pass judge and below the multi-trait baseline.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Lock the rubric before scoring. Part 2's criteria become a different measurement if the judge reinterprets them on every call. The hash in the bundle is the version.
- Evidence is a checklist decision plus a citation, on a three-point scale, not a holistic impression. That is a concrete alternative to "score this from 1 to 6."
- A couple of hundred labeled examples can map judge signals onto a human scale. Part 4's calibration step is doing real work here, and it is not free of labels.
- The same calibration applied to a holistic score does not reproduce the full method. The checklist still matters, and on one dataset at the smaller calibration size it does not win.
- Cost is visible. The evidence-grounded judge spends more tokens than a single pass. Part 2's quality, latency, and cost comparison applies to the judge, not only to the system being judged.

## Limits

This is not an agent-trajectory paper. There is no tool use. Instability and audit coverage are defined and never given a number. Figure 3's robustness bars have no printed QWK. WebNLG is scored against a sum of trait ratings the authors built. A bad source rubric is preserved, not repaired. Each new task needs its own bundle and its own calibration map. The authors say the method is not a replacement for expert judgment in high-stakes use, and the calibration does not come with a fairness result across groups.

figures.alt: Three columns. Phase I locks a human rubric into traits, a checklist, evidence rules, and a hash. Phase II marks each checklist item 0, 1, or 2 and cites a sentence or span. Phase III fits a ridge model on a calibration set and maps the result onto the human score scale. The example ends at a final score of 4 out of 6.

Columns are direct holistic scoring, multi-trait scoring, AutoScore, CheckEval, and RULERS, across four backbones. RULERS is highest in every row except the two SummHF rows that use Llama, where CheckEval is higher.
figures.caption: Table 2 from Hong et al. (2026). The highest cell is Llama-3.1-70B on ASAP 2.0, 0.7179 ± 0.0055. The two SummHF Llama rows are the exceptions.

figures.alt: A grid of score densities, four datasets by four backbones. Pink histograms are human scores. Curves are direct holistic scoring, multi-trait scoring, AutoScore, CheckEval, and RULERS. Axes differ by dataset, including 1–6, 1–7, 0–15, and 3–9.

sources.title: PReMISE: Policy Rubrics as Measurement Specifications for LLM Judges
sources.abstract: LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate open-ended responses, but their scores depend strongly on the rubrics that condition them. A vague rubric asking for a response to be ``helpful and factual'' can reward polished answers that invent facts or violate user intent. We treat reusable rubrics as measurement specifications: changing the rubric changes the response quality measurement induced by a fixed judge. We introduce PReMISE, a framework that, given pairwise human-preference data, (i) discovers a policy-level rubric set, and (ii) audits any rubric set under LLM-judge use along four axes: structural adequacy, reliability, preference fit, and adversarial robustness. Across rubric sources no raw source is simultaneously reliable, preference-predictive, and adversarially robust; and high inter-rater agreement does not imply low exploitability. PReMISE is the only rubric source to score non-trivially on applicability, specificity, and effective dimensionality simultaneously. We contribute two audit-targeted repair operations: preference-rank selection raises judge accuracy on paired responses from $65.0\%$ to $68.6\%$, competitive with the strongest rubric-discovery baselines and leading on two of three judges in our cross-judge sweep; reliability-constrained refinement reduces the rate at which exploit responses receive high scores from $46.4\%$ to $36.0\%$ with little change in inter-judge agreement ($\alpha{=}.531\to.519$).
sources.summary: PReMISE treats a reusable rubric as a measurement specification and audits it for structure, stability, preference fit, and how easily an attacker can satisfy it. No rubric source in the audit leads every column, and the repair that raises preference accuracy is not the repair that lowers exploitability.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Roy, Pujari, Kumarage, and colleagues study the rubric that is reused across many prompts, the kind of policy sheet Part 2 asks a team to write, rather than an answer key for one item. PReMISE is a discover, audit, and repair pipeline for that sheet. The tutorial question is whether a rubric that judges agree on is the same thing as a rubric that measures what you meant, and whether it can be gamed. That is Part 4.

## What they did

A policy rubric is a set of criteria meant to apply across prompts. For a fixed judge and a rubric, each criterion returns a score. Here the scale used in the audit is 0 to 10. Discovery reads pairwise preferences, asks a model for candidate criteria, clusters near-duplicates, and keeps a compact set. The audit has four axes, kept separate rather than collapsed into one index. Structure is five design properties, scored by a majority of three models. Reliability is inter-judge agreement (Krippendorff's α), a flip rate under repeated sampling, and stability under paraphrase. Preference fit asks whether the criteria fire on the prompts they claim to cover, and whether a judge using them picks the human-preferred response. Adversarial robustness is a verified fool rate: an attacker tries to satisfy a criterion, the judge scores the attempt at least 7 out of 10, and a separate verifier, blind to the attack, calls it an exploit.

Two repairs do different jobs. Preference-rank selection keeps criteria that point the same way as the human preference and does not rewrite the text. The robustness repair edits the text, with a length budget, and is accepted when the fool rate falls without giving up too much agreement. The audit uses four preference corpora. The held-out accuracy test uses three judges, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-32B, and Kimi K2.5, each asked either for one A-or-B verdict or for a score on every criterion.

{{figure:fig2-workflow.png}}

## What they found

Table 1 averages the audit across the four corpora. No source leads every column. Auto-Rubric has the highest preference accuracy in that table, 68.7, and the lowest verified fool rate, 0.272. AgentEval has the highest agreement, α = 0.582. Discovered PReMISE is strong on specificity and on how many distinct directions the scores actually use, and it is not the accuracy leader.

Figure 4 is that anatomy on UltraFeedback. PReMISE criteria fire on 58% of in-domain prompts, the in-domain rate is 7.5 points above the out-of-domain rate, and the effective dimensionality is 15 out of 20. AgentEval and Inverse CAI fire widely and are slightly more applicable out of domain than in it. Auto-Rubric fires on 3% of prompts.

Preference-rank selection moves the Table 1 preference accuracy from 65.0 to 68.6, a tenth of a point under Auto-Rubric's 68.7. On the per-judge table, that repaired rubric is below a no-rubric baseline for Qwen3-32B's direct verdict, 65.8 against 66.4. Discovered PReMISE, before that repair, is below the no-rubric baseline on every direct-verdict column. The robustness repair moves the other direction: verified fool rate from 0.464 to 0.360, with α from 0.531 to 0.519, and preference accuracy does not rise.

{{figure:table1-audit.png}}

{{figure:fig4-anatomy.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A rubric is a measurement specification. Agreement among judges, fit to preferences, and resistance to a written exploit are different columns. Part 4 should not treat one of them as a proxy for the others.
- The repair that chases preference accuracy narrows which prompts the criteria apply to. The repair that chases exploits edits the wording and does not buy accuracy. A team in Part 2 has to say which axis it is optimizing.
- A discovered rubric can lose to no rubric at all. Adding criteria is not automatically a better judge.
- On one of the three judges, the preference repair itself loses to the no-rubric baseline. A rubric tuned on a large judge is not guaranteed on a smaller one.
- High α is a stability check. The paper says it is not evidence that the rubric matches a human's idea of quality.

## Limits

The pipeline is for rubrics that are supposed to track pairwise preferences. Safety floors and hard constraints that should override a preference are out of scope. The fool rate is a lower bound under this attacker, judge, and verifier; the verifier's precision against a three-annotator majority is 72.7%. Absolute numbers are judge-relative. The authors do not test the rubrics as a training reward, and they say consequential per-item decisions would still need human calibration.

figures.alt: A three-stage diagram. Discovery extracts and consolidates criteria from pairwise preferences. A four-axis audit scores structural adequacy, reliability, preference fit, and adversarial robustness. Targeted repair either reselects criteria or edits text, then sends the rubric back for another audit.

figures.alt: A cross-source audit table. Columns cover structure, agreement, flip rate, paraphrase stability, verified fool rate, applicability, specificity, effective dimensionality, preference accuracy, and a Bradley-Terry diagnostic. No row is best in every column. Auto-Rubric's preference accuracy is 68.7. Preference-repaired PReMISE is 68.6. Discovered PReMISE is 65.0.
